title: Lincoln elected president
summary: Abraham Lincoln of the new Republican Party wins the presidency with about 40 per cent of the vote, in a four-way race. He is not even on the ballot in ten southern states. He promises to leave slavery alone where it exists, but to stop it spreading into the western territories.
significance: Lincoln won without a single southern electoral vote. To many white southerners, a president elected by the North alone, and hostile to slavery, was reason enough to leave the Union.

title: South Carolina secedes
summary: A convention in Charleston votes 169 to 0 to leave the Union. Four days later it publishes its reasons, naming the North's hostility to slavery again and again. Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana and Texas follow by 1 February.
significance: The first state to go. In the Deep South, where nearly half the people were enslaved, the slave economy was at the heart of the decision.

title: The Confederate States are formed
summary: Delegates from the seceded states meet in Montgomery and adopt a constitution for the Confederate States of America. It protects slavery by name. Jefferson Davis of Mississippi is chosen president and sworn in on 18 February.
significance: In March vice president Alexander Stephens said the new government's 'cornerstone' was the belief that slavery was the Black man's natural condition.

title: Lincoln is sworn in
summary: Lincoln takes the oath in front of the unfinished Capitol dome. He says secession is illegal, promises not to touch slavery in the states, and tells the South the choice of war is theirs. Federal forts in the South are now his problem.
significance: Only two forts in the seceded states were still in Union hands that mattered: Fort Pickens at Pensacola and Fort Sumter at Charleston.

title: Fort Sumter
stat: No one killed in the bombardment. Two Union soldiers died when a gun exploded during the salute as the fort was handed over
summary: Lincoln sends supplies to the garrison of Fort Sumter. Before dawn on 12 April, Confederate guns around the harbour open fire. After 34 hours, Major Robert Anderson surrenders.
significance: The war had begun. Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers to put down the rebellion, and the North rallied to the flag.

title: Virginia secedes
summary: Asked to send troops against the Deep South, Virginia's convention votes to secede instead. Arkansas, Tennessee and North Carolina follow in May. Robert E. Lee, offered a senior Union command, resigns and goes with his state.
significance: Virginia brought the South's biggest factory, the Tredegar Iron Works, and its best general. The Confederate capital moved to Richmond, only 100 miles from Washington.

title: Riot in Baltimore
summary: The 6th Massachusetts, on its way to defend Washington, has to change trains by marching across Baltimore. A pro-southern crowd attacks with stones and pistols, and the soldiers fire back. Four soldiers and twelve civilians are killed.
significance: Maryland surrounds Washington on three sides. Lincoln sent troops to occupy Baltimore, suspended habeas corpus and jailed suspected secessionists to keep the state in the Union.

title: The blockade and the Anaconda Plan
summary: Lincoln declares a blockade of every southern port, 3,500 miles of coast. General Winfield Scott proposes to squeeze the South like a snake: close its ports, take the Mississippi, and wait. The press mocks it as the Anaconda Plan.
significance: The navy had about 40 working ships in 1861 and some 500 by 1865. Fast blockade runners kept getting through, but cotton exports collapsed and the South ran short of almost everything.

title: Fort Monroe: 'contraband of war'
summary: Three enslaved men, Frank Baker, Shepard Mallory and James Townsend, row across to the Union fort at the tip of the Virginia peninsula. Their owner demands them back. General Benjamin Butler refuses, calling them 'contraband of war'.
significance: Word spread fast. Thousands of enslaved people fled to Union lines, forcing the government to decide what freedom meant long before Lincoln announced emancipation.

title: First Battle of Bull Run
summary: General Irvin McDowell's raw Union army marches on the Confederates at Manassas Junction, with picnicking spectators from Washington behind. After a morning of success, the attack stalls at Henry House Hill. Thomas Jackson's brigade stands 'like a stone wall', fresh Confederate troops arrive by rail, and the Union army breaks.
significance: The first big battle ended any hope of a short war. The North called for 500,000 three-year volunteers.

title: Wilson's Creek
summary: Nathaniel Lyon attacks a larger force of Confederates and Missouri State Guard. Lyon is killed, the first Union general to die in the war, and his army retreats. Sterling Price's Missourians hold the south-west of the state into the winter.
significance: Missouri stayed in the Union, but it became a land of guerrilla war, neighbour against neighbour, for four years.

title: Port Royal Sound
summary: Flag Officer Samuel Du Pont's fleet steams in circles past two Confederate forts, firing as it goes, and silences them in an afternoon. White planters flee the Sea Islands. About 10,000 enslaved people stay behind.
significance: The blockade gained a deep harbour in the heart of the South. On the islands, teachers and freedpeople began the Port Royal Experiment: schools, wages and land for the formerly enslaved.

title: Forts Henry and Donelson
summary: Ulysses S. Grant and the river gunboats take Fort Henry on the Tennessee River on 6 February, then besiege Fort Donelson on the Cumberland. When the Confederate commander asks for terms, Grant replies: no terms except unconditional and immediate surrender.
significance: The North's first big victory. It opened two rivers into the South, forced the Confederates out of Kentucky and Nashville, and made Grant famous.

title: Pea Ridge
summary: Samuel Curtis's Union army beats a larger Confederate force under Earl Van Dorn in the Ozark hills. Two Cherokee regiments, one led by Stand Watie, fight on the Confederate side.
significance: Missouri was safe from invasion until 1864. Van Dorn's army was sent east of the Mississippi, leaving Arkansas thinly defended.

title: Monitor and Virginia
summary: On 8 March the Confederate ironclad Virginia, built on the hull of the old Merrimack, sinks the Cumberland and burns the Congress. The next morning the strange Union ironclad Monitor, 'a cheesebox on a raft', arrives. The two fight for four hours and neither can sink the other.
significance: The first battle between ironclad ships. Navies around the world saw that their wooden fleets were out of date overnight.

title: Glorieta Pass
summary: Henry Sibley's Texans have marched up the Rio Grande and taken Albuquerque and Santa Fe. At Glorieta Pass they push back Colorado volunteers, but a Union party gets behind them and burns their wagon train. Without supplies, they retreat to Texas.
significance: It ended the Confederate dream of a southern route to the gold of Colorado and the ports of California.

title: McClellan's Peninsula Campaign
summary: George McClellan ships about 120,000 men down the Chesapeake to Fort Monroe, to march on Richmond from the east. A much smaller Confederate force holds him at Yorktown for a month. By late May his army is within sight of Richmond's church spires.
significance: McClellan was a fine organiser but always believed he was outnumbered. When General Joseph Johnston was wounded on 31 May, Robert E. Lee took command.

title: Shiloh
stat: About 23,700 killed, wounded or missing in two days, more than in all America's earlier wars put together
summary: Albert Sidney Johnston's army surprises Grant's camps at dawn and drives them back to the Tennessee River. Johnston is killed in the afternoon. Overnight Don Carlos Buell's army arrives, and on the second day the Confederates are pushed back to Corinth.
significance: Shiloh showed both sides what the war would cost. Grant said afterwards he gave up hope of saving the Union except by complete conquest.

title: New Orleans falls
summary: David Farragut's fleet runs past Forts Jackson and St Philip in the dark on 24 April, through fire rafts and a Confederate flotilla. The next day it anchors off New Orleans, the South's largest city. Union troops under Benjamin Butler take over on 1 May.
significance: The Confederacy lost its biggest port and the mouth of the Mississippi in the first year of the war.

title: Stonewall Jackson in the Shenandoah
summary: With about 17,000 men, Stonewall Jackson marches up and down the Shenandoah Valley, beating three separate Union armies in a month. At Winchester on 25 May he routs Nathaniel Banks.
significance: Lincoln held back troops meant for McClellan to protect Washington. Jackson then slipped away to join Lee outside Richmond.

title: The Seven Days
stat: About 36,000 killed, wounded or missing in a week
summary: Lee attacks McClellan's army day after day from 25 June. McClellan retreats to the James River. At Malvern Hill on 1 July, Union guns cut down the Confederate attacks, but McClellan keeps falling back.
significance: Lee saved Richmond and took the war to the North. The failure turned Lincoln towards harder war, and towards emancipation.

title: The Dakota War in Minnesota
stat: Hundreds of settlers killed; 38 Dakota men hanged at Mankato
summary: Starving, cheated of treaty payments and told by a trader to 'eat grass', Dakota warriors attack the agency and the farms around it. Hundreds of settlers are killed in six weeks. After the army wins, 38 Dakota men are hanged together at Mankato on 26 December.
significance: The largest mass execution in American history. The Dakota were expelled from Minnesota, and war spread onto the northern plains.

title: Second Battle of Bull Run
summary: John Pope's new Army of Virginia attacks Jackson's men behind an unfinished railway cut. On 30 August James Longstreet's corps, which Pope does not know is there, smashes into his flank. Pope's army retreats to Washington.
significance: In three months Lee had driven two Union armies away from Richmond. He decided to invade the North.

title: Antietam
stat: About 22,700 killed, wounded or missing: the bloodiest single day in American history
summary: Union soldiers find a copy of Lee's orders wrapped round three cigars, and McClellan catches Lee's army along Antietam Creek. The fighting moves from the Cornfield to the Sunken Road to Burnside's Bridge. Lee is battered but escapes back to Virginia.
significance: Not a crushing win, but enough. It kept Britain and France from recognising the Confederacy and gave Lincoln the victory he needed to announce emancipation.

title: Lincoln announces emancipation
summary: Five days after Antietam, Lincoln warns the rebel states: if they are still fighting on 1 January 1863, everyone enslaved there will be 'thenceforward, and forever free'.
significance: The war for the Union became a war against slavery too. Lincoln had drafted the order in July but waited for a victory, so it would not look like a cry of despair.

title: Perryville
summary: Braxton Bragg's Confederates have invaded Kentucky and installed a governor at Frankfort. They meet Buell's army near Perryville in a fight over water in a drought. Bragg wins the field but retreats to Tennessee.
significance: Kentucky stayed in the Union. Lincoln is said to have remarked that he hoped to have God on his side, but he must have Kentucky.

title: Fredericksburg
summary: Ambrose Burnside crosses the Rappahannock on pontoon bridges and sends wave after wave against Confederates behind a stone wall on Marye's Heights. Not one Union soldier reaches the wall. Watching, Lee says it is well that war is so terrible, or we should grow too fond of it.
significance: The North's lowest point of the war so far. Morale in the Army of the Potomac collapsed over the winter.

title: Stones River
summary: On New Year's Eve Bragg's Confederates drive William Rosecrans's army back to the Nashville Pike. Rosecrans holds on. When Bragg attacks again on 2 January, massed Union guns stop him, and he retreats.
significance: Nearly a third of each army was killed or wounded. Lincoln wrote to Rosecrans that the nation could hardly have lived over another defeat.

title: The Emancipation Proclamation
summary: Lincoln signs the proclamation: everyone held as a slave in the rebel states is free. It does not cover the loyal border states or Union-held Tennessee. It also opens the army and navy to Black men.
significance: It freed no one the army could not reach, but every Union advance after this day was an army of liberation. Black churches across the North held all-night 'watch meetings' to wait for it.

title: Richmond bread riot
summary: Prices in Richmond have risen about tenfold. Several hundred women, many of them wives of workers and soldiers, march through the business district with axes and knives, breaking into stores for bread and meat. Jefferson Davis climbs on a wagon and orders them to go home.
significance: Shortages, the draft and the blockade turned many poorer white southerners against the war. Similar riots broke out in Atlanta, Mobile and other cities.

title: Grant crosses the Mississippi
summary: After months of failed attempts on Vicksburg, Grant marches his army down the Louisiana bank while gunboats run past the city's batteries at night. On 30 April they ferry about 22,000 men across to Bruinsburg, below the city.
significance: In the next three weeks Grant won five battles, took Jackson, the state capital, and drove the Confederates inside Vicksburg's defences.

title: Chancellorsville
summary: Joseph Hooker's 130,000 men outflank Lee's 60,000. Lee splits his army and sends Stonewall Jackson on a 12-mile march round the Union right, which collapses at dusk on 2 May. That night Jackson is shot by his own men in the dark.
significance: Lee's greatest victory, and his costliest loss. Jackson died of pneumonia on 10 May.

title: The United States Colored Troops
stat: About 179,000 Black soldiers served, one in ten of the Union army, and about 19,000 Black sailors
summary: The War Department sets up a Bureau of Colored Troops to raise Black regiments. Most of the men have escaped from slavery. They serve under white officers and are paid less than white soldiers until 1864.
significance: Black soldiers fought in some of the war's hardest battles. The Confederacy threatened to enslave or kill them if captured, and refused to exchange them as prisoners.

title: Harriet Tubman's Combahee River raid
summary: Guided by Harriet Tubman's network of scouts, Union gunboats carrying Black soldiers steam up the Combahee River. They burn rice plantations, and enslaved people run to the boats. More than 700 are carried away to freedom.
significance: Tubman, who had led dozens of people out of slavery before the war, became the first woman to help lead an armed raid in the war.

title: Gettysburg: the first two days
summary: Lee invades Pennsylvania. On 1 July his men meet Union cavalry west of Gettysburg and drive two Union corps back through the town to Cemetery Hill. On 2 July Longstreet attacks the Union left at the Peach Orchard, the Wheatfield and Little Round Top, and nearly breaks it.
significance: George Meade, in command for only three days, kept his army on the high ground in a fish-hook line from Culp's Hill to the Round Tops.

title: Gettysburg: Pickett's Charge
stat: Three days: about 51,000 killed, wounded, captured or missing. About half of the 12,500 men in Pickett's Charge fell or were captured
summary: After a two-hour cannonade, about 12,500 Confederates march a mile across open fields towards the centre of the Union line. Cannon and rifle fire cut them down. A few hundred cross the stone wall at the Angle before they are killed or captured.
significance: Lee retreated to Virginia and never invaded the North again. The spot became known as the 'high-water mark of the Confederacy'.

title: Vicksburg surrenders
stat: About 29,500 Confederates surrendered after a 47-day siege
summary: Shelled day and night, with civilians living in caves and eating mules, John Pemberton's garrison surrenders on Independence Day. Port Hudson, the last Confederate fort on the river, gives up five days later.
significance: The Mississippi was open from end to end and the Confederacy cut in two. Lincoln wrote that 'the Father of Waters again goes unvexed to the sea'.

title: New York draft riots
place: Third Avenue and 47th Street, New York
stat: At least 119 killed, perhaps many more
summary: The first names are drawn under the new federal draft, which lets the rich buy their way out for $300. Mobs, many of them poor Irish immigrants, burn the draft office, then turn on Black New Yorkers. They lynch Black men in the streets and burn the Colored Orphan Asylum.
significance: Troops fresh from Gettysburg put down the riots after four days. It remains the worst civil disorder in American history.

title: The 54th Massachusetts at Fort Wagner
stat: The 54th lost about 270 of its 600 men
summary: The 54th Massachusetts, one of the first Black regiments raised in the North, leads a night assault along a narrow beach against a sand fort. Its colonel, Robert Gould Shaw, is killed on the parapet. Sergeant William Carney carries the flag back despite four wounds.
significance: The attack failed, but the courage of the 54th was reported across the North and helped silence doubts about Black soldiers.

title: The Lawrence massacre
stat: About 150 men and boys killed, by some counts nearly 200
summary: William Quantrill's pro-Confederate guerrillas ride into Lawrence, the anti-slavery stronghold of Kansas, at dawn. They kill almost every man and boy they find and burn the town.
significance: The worst atrocity of the border war. The Union army replied by forcing almost everyone out of four Missouri border counties.

title: Chickamauga
summary: Bragg, reinforced by Longstreet's corps sent by rail from Virginia, attacks Rosecrans in the woods south of Chattanooga. A mistaken order opens a gap in the Union line just as Longstreet attacks it. George Thomas holds Snodgrass Hill until dark, earning the name 'the Rock of Chickamauga'.
significance: The biggest Confederate victory in the west. Rosecrans's army fell back into Chattanooga and was besieged there.

title: The Gettysburg Address
summary: At the opening of a cemetery for the Union dead, Lincoln speaks for about two minutes after a two-hour oration. He calls for 'a new birth of freedom', so that government of the people, by the people, for the people shall not perish from the earth.
significance: In about 270 words Lincoln recast the war as a test of whether a nation built on equality could survive.

title: Chattanooga: Missionary Ridge
summary: Grant arrives, opens a supply line and gathers reinforcements. On 24 November Union troops take Lookout Mountain in fog. The next day Thomas's men, ordered only to take the rifle pits at the foot of Missionary Ridge, keep climbing without orders and break Bragg's line.
significance: Chattanooga, the gateway to Georgia, was secure. In March 1864 Lincoln brought Grant east to command all the Union armies.

title: The Hunley sinks the Housatonic
summary: The Confederate submarine H. L. Hunley, hand-cranked by a crew of eight, rams a torpedo into the Union warship Housatonic outside Charleston harbour. The Housatonic sinks in minutes. The Hunley never comes home.
significance: The first submarine to sink a warship. The Hunley was found in 1995 and raised in 2000, with her crew still at their stations.

title: Andersonville prison opens
stat: About 45,000 Union prisoners held; nearly 13,000 died
summary: The first Union prisoners arrive at a stockade in the Georgia pine woods built for 10,000. By August it holds about 33,000. A sluggish stream is both their water supply and their sewer, and men die of disease, exposure and hunger.
significance: Prisoner exchanges had broken down, partly because the Confederacy refused to exchange Black soldiers. The camp's commander, Henry Wirz, was hanged for war crimes in November 1865.

title: Fort Pillow massacre
summary: Nathan Bedford Forrest's cavalry storms a Union fort on the Mississippi held by about 600 men, half of them Black soldiers. Many are shot after they try to surrender. About two-thirds of the Black troops are killed.
significance: 'Remember Fort Pillow' became a battle cry for Black regiments. Forrest later became the first leader of the Ku Klux Klan.

title: The Wilderness and Spotsylvania
summary: Grant crosses the Rapidan and Lee strikes him in dense second-growth forest. The woods catch fire and wounded men burn. After two days Grant does not retreat as his predecessors did. He marches south, and at Spotsylvania on 12 May the two armies fight hand to hand for almost a day at the 'Bloody Angle'.
significance: The Overland Campaign had begun: six weeks of almost constant fighting that cost the Union about 55,000 casualties and Lee about 33,000, men he could not replace.

title: Cold Harbor
summary: Grant orders a dawn attack on Lee's entrenchments ten miles from Richmond. Some soldiers pin their names to their coats so their bodies can be identified. Thousands fall in under an hour, and the attack achieves nothing.
significance: Grant wrote that it was the one assault he always regretted. He changed course and slipped across the James River towards Petersburg.

title: The siege of Petersburg begins
summary: Grant's army crosses the James and attacks Petersburg, the rail hub that feeds Richmond. Hesitant attacks miss a chance to take it, and Lee's army arrives. Both sides dig in.
significance: The siege lasted nine and a half months, a war of trenches and mines that looked ahead to 1914. Grant kept stretching Lee's lines until they broke.

title: Lincoln under fire at Fort Stevens
summary: Jubal Early's Confederates march down the Shenandoah Valley, brush aside a small force at Monocacy and reach the edge of Washington. Lincoln comes to watch from the parapet of Fort Stevens and stands in the open under fire until an officer shouts at him to get down.
significance: The only time a serving president came under enemy fire in battle. Veterans rushed up from Petersburg, and Early withdrew.

title: The Battle of the Crater
summary: Pennsylvania coal miners dig a 500-foot tunnel under the Confederate line and blow it up with four tons of gunpowder. The Black division trained to lead the attack is replaced at the last minute. White troops pour into the crater instead of round it, and are trapped.
significance: A great chance thrown away. When the Black division was finally sent in, many of its men were killed after they surrendered.

title: Mobile Bay
summary: Farragut's fleet steams into Mobile Bay past Fort Morgan. The monitor Tecumseh hits a mine, then called a torpedo, and sinks in seconds. Farragut, lashed to the rigging of his flagship, orders the fleet on, in words later remembered as 'Damn the torpedoes!'
significance: The last big Gulf port open to blockade runners was closed. The forts fell by 23 August, though the city of Mobile held out until April 1865.

title: Atlanta falls
summary: Since May, William Tecumseh Sherman has pushed south from Chattanooga, flanking Joseph Johnston out of one position after another. Johnston's replacement, John Bell Hood, attacks and loses three battles. When Sherman cuts the last railway, Hood abandons the city. Sherman wires Washington: 'Atlanta is ours, and fairly won.'
significance: With the war stuck at Petersburg, the North had been close to despair, and Lincoln expected to lose the election. Atlanta changed the mood overnight.

title: Sheridan in the Shenandoah
summary: Philip Sheridan has beaten Early twice and burned the barns and mills of the Shenandoah Valley, the granary of Lee's army. At dawn on 19 October Early surprises his camps at Cedar Creek. Sheridan rides twenty miles from Winchester, rallies his men and routs Early by evening.
significance: The valley that had fed Confederate armies and hidden their raids was wrecked. Locals called the autumn of 1864 'the Burning'.

title: Lincoln re-elected
summary: Lincoln beats George McClellan, his old general, who ran on a Democratic platform calling for peace talks. Lincoln wins 55 per cent of the vote and all but three states. Soldiers, many voting in camp, back him by about three to one.
significance: The North had voted to fight on until the Union was restored and slavery destroyed. It was the first national election ever held in the middle of a civil war.

title: Sherman's March to the Sea
summary: Sherman burns Atlanta's railways and factories, and much of the town with them, then cuts loose from his supply lines. About 62,000 men march for Savannah, 300 miles away, in two wings, living off the land and wrecking railways, mills and plantations in a band up to 60 miles wide.
significance: Sherman set out to show that the Confederacy could not protect its own people. Thousands of enslaved people followed his columns to freedom.

title: The Sand Creek massacre
stat: Between about 150 and 230 Cheyenne and Arapaho killed, most of them women, children and old people
summary: Colonel John Chivington's Colorado volunteers attack a camp of Cheyenne and Arapaho who believe they are under army protection. Their chief, Black Kettle, flies an American flag over his lodge. The soldiers kill and mutilate people as they flee up the dry creek bed.
significance: Congress condemned the massacre, but no one was punished. It set off years of war on the southern plains.

title: Franklin and Nashville
stat: At Franklin about 6,000 Confederate casualties in five hours, including six generals killed
summary: Hood marches into Tennessee hoping to draw Sherman back. At Franklin he throws his army across two miles of open ground against Union earthworks. Two weeks later, on 15 and 16 December, George Thomas attacks Hood's shattered army at Nashville and routs it.
significance: The Confederate Army of Tennessee was destroyed as a fighting force. The war in the west was over.

title: Savannah: a Christmas gift
summary: Sherman's men storm Fort McAllister on 13 December and make contact with the navy. Savannah's defenders slip away across the river, and the mayor surrenders the city. Sherman telegraphs Lincoln, offering him Savannah as a Christmas gift.
significance: The march had cut the Confederacy in two again. In January Sherman turned north into the Carolinas.

title: 'Forty acres': Special Field Order No. 15
summary: After meeting twenty Black ministers in Savannah, who tell him that freedom means owning land, Sherman sets aside the Sea Islands and the coast for freed families. Each can claim up to forty acres. About 40,000 people settle there.
significance: President Andrew Johnson cancelled the order in the autumn of 1865 and returned most of the land to its former owners. 'Forty acres and a mule' became a symbol of a promise broken.

title: Fort Fisher
summary: After the heaviest naval bombardment of the war, soldiers and sailors storm the great sand fort guarding Wilmington. Wilmington itself falls on 22 February.
significance: The last major port for blockade runners was closed. Lee's army had lived on supplies brought in through Wilmington.

title: Petersburg and Richmond fall
summary: Sheridan breaks Lee's right at Five Forks on 1 April, and the next morning Grant attacks all along the Petersburg line. Lee's army and the Confederate government flee that night, setting fire to Richmond's warehouses. On 3 April Union troops, Black regiments among the first, march in.
significance: On 4 April Lincoln walked through the burning capital, surrounded by freed people who reached out to touch him.

title: Lee surrenders at Appomattox
place: McLean House, Appomattox Court House, Virginia
summary: Lee's starving army tries to escape west, but Union cavalry blocks the road. In the parlour of Wilmer McLean's house, Lee surrenders to Grant. Grant lets the men go home on parole and keep their horses for the spring ploughing.
significance: The Confederacy's main army was gone. Other armies held out for weeks, but the war was effectively over.

title: Lincoln is shot
summary: On Good Friday the actor John Wilkes Booth, a Confederate sympathiser, shoots Lincoln in the back of the head during a comedy at Ford's Theatre. An accomplice stabs the Secretary of State, William Seward, at home. Lincoln dies the next morning in a boarding house across the street.
significance: Booth was cornered and shot in a Virginia barn on 26 April. Lincoln's death left Reconstruction to Andrew Johnson, a southern Democrat with little sympathy for the freed people.

title: Johnston surrenders at Bennett Place
stat: About 89,000 soldiers in the Carolinas, Georgia and Florida, the largest surrender of the war
summary: Joseph Johnston, defying Jefferson Davis's order to fight on, meets Sherman at a small farmhouse and surrenders his army. Their first, generous agreement is rejected in Washington, and Johnston signs Grant's Appomattox terms instead.
significance: Most Confederate troops east of the Mississippi were now out of the war. Richard Taylor surrendered in Alabama on 4 May.

title: The Sultana disaster
stat: About 1,168 killed, by some counts many more
summary: The steamboat Sultana, licensed for 376 passengers, is crammed with more than 2,000 Union soldiers just freed from Andersonville and Cahaba prison camps. A patched boiler explodes at 2 a.m. north of Memphis, and the boat burns to the waterline.
significance: The worst maritime disaster in American history, almost forgotten at the time in the news of Lincoln's death.

title: Freedom in Texas: Juneteenth
summary: Two weeks after the last Confederate army in Texas surrenders, General Gordon Granger lands at Galveston and reads General Order No. 3: all slaves are free. About 250,000 people in Texas hear the news.
significance: Freed Texans celebrated the day every year. Juneteenth became a federal holiday in 2021.

title: The last Confederate general surrenders
summary: Edmund Kirby Smith has given up the Confederate armies west of the Mississippi on 2 June. Stand Watie, a Cherokee leader and Confederate brigadier general, is the last to surrender, at Doaksville in Indian Territory.
significance: The war split the Cherokee and Creek nations in two. Afterwards the United States treated all five nations as defeated enemies and took much of their land.

title: The Thirteenth Amendment
summary: Georgia becomes the 27th state to ratify the amendment that Congress passed on 31 January, and it becomes law. Slavery is abolished everywhere in the United States, including the loyal states of Kentucky and Delaware.
significance: About four million people were free. What freedom would mean, in votes, land and safety, was the struggle of Reconstruction and the century after.
